sources.title: Cesar A. Fortes-Lima and colleagues, The genetic legacy of the expansion of Bantu-speaking peoples in Africa, Nature (2023 online; 2024 volume)
sources.note: Full indexed original article read. Abstract dates initial expansion broadly 6000 to 4000 years ago, identifies interaction and gene flow rather than isolated uniform populations. Main text describes more than 500 languages and complex histories. Public account does not equate language, genes, race or political territory.

sources.title: Rebecca Grollemund, David Schoenbrun and Jan Vansina, Moving Histories: Bantu Language Expansions, Eclectic Economies, and Mobilities, Journal of African History (2023)
sources.note: Direct original research read. Printed pages 29 and 33 to 35, PDF pages 17 and 21 to 23, reject equating Urewe ceramics, earliest farming, ironworking and the first Bantu speakers. Their specific alternative migration chronology is not treated as consensus.

sources.title: Katharina Neumann, Barbara Eichhorn and Hans-Peter Wotzka, Iron Age plant subsistence in the Inner Congo Basin (DR Congo), Vegetation History and Archaeobotany (2022)
sources.note: Direct original archaeological study read: Iyonda Imbonga-phase millet, tuber tissue, germinated millet and possible brewing, and Bolondo raised house platforms from the mid-fourteenth century. Radiocarbon uncertainty retained. No cassava or maize projected into prehistoric African foodways.

sources.title: Madeleine Bleasdale and colleagues, Isotopic and microbotanical insights into Iron Age agricultural reliance in the Central African rainforest (2020)
sources.note: Full relevant indexed discussion read; direct page returned browser challenge. Discussion reports fish-dominated faunal assemblage at Bolondo, forest/freshwater dietary signals and millet present but not a straightforward dietary staple. Does not prove every individual ate an identical diet.

sources.title: Revisiting Kalundu Mound, Zambia: Implications for the Timing of Social and Subsistence Transitions in Iron Age Southern Africa, African Archaeological Review (2021)
sources.note: Direct original research read. Crop results: finger millet and sorghum, with one sorghum grain directly dated to cal AD 1320 to 1415. Discussion: multiple potential uses of finger millet and good storage; Isamu Pati grain bins interpreted as likely millet stores. These interpretations are qualified.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Zimbabwe National Monument
sources.note: Institutional description read in full indexed result. Great Enclosure dated fourteenth century, cut-granite walls and daga living quarters with kitchens, living huts and courts. Does not repeat the page’s outdated unqualified environmental-collapse account, Queen of Sheba myth, or problematic dating of all Valley Ruins.

sources.title: Stephanie Wynne-Jones, The public life of the Swahili stonehouse, 14th to 15th centuries AD, Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 32 (2013), 759 to 773
sources.note: Full indexed House 44 section read from the author’s institutional repository; direct PDF timed out. House 44 construction, plaster floors, porites doorframes, earthen back room, midden and southwest latrine infilled when a fresh sand layer was added. No flushing, sewer network or universal indoor toilet claimed.

sources.title: Zanzibari narrators and Edward Steere, Swahili Tales, as Told by Natives of Zanzibar, with an English Translation (1870)
sources.note: Direct original-edition OCR read. Printed pages 370 to 371, opening of Sungura na Simba, have Nani ninyi? and Who are you? clearly legible in OCR; capitalization and question mark retained. The 1870 printed witness is not claimed as an ancient inscription. Preface describes narrator improvisation; racist essentialist claims in that preface are not endorsed.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Shared broad linguistic-history narrative, not a political alias or assertion of continuous control. The earliest polygon stretches far beyond a defensible Bantu-speaking distribution, while later polygons omit many relevant areas. The opening warns that the named archaeological and later writing examples do not all fall inside either imported polygon or time window. The present distribution of languages cannot be back-projected unchanged.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Exact short Swahili dialogue in the 1870 original bilingual edition, with matching translation; explicitly later than both map intervals. No invented Proto-Bantu written sample.
